questions.question: What distinguishes semantic segmentation from object detection?

options.text: Segmentation predicts bounding boxes; detection predicts pixels
Segmentation assigns a class label to every pixel; detection localizes object instances with boxes
They are the same task
Segmentation only works on grayscale images

questions.explanation: Semantic segmentation produces per-pixel class labels; object detection outputs bounding boxes per instance.

questions.question: What is the purpose of U-Net's skip connections?

options.text: To combine high-resolution encoder features with upsampled decoder features
To reduce the number of parameters
To skip training unnecessary layers
To implement residual learning like ResNet

questions.explanation: Skip connections preserve spatial detail from the encoder and fuse it with the decoder's upsampled features, improving localization.

questions.question: In DeepLab, why are atrous (dilated) convolutions used?

options.text: To reduce inference time via sparser kernels
To preserve feature map resolution while enlarging the receptive field
To replace pooling entirely with learnable layers
To enable color-space augmentation

questions.explanation: DeepLab uses atrous convolutions to capture multi-scale context without downsampling the feature maps.

questions.question: Which loss is commonly used to handle severe class imbalance in segmentation?

options.text: Mean Squared Error
Dice loss or focal loss
Hinge loss
KL divergence

questions.explanation: Dice and focal losses directly address class imbalance by emphasizing under-represented regions or hard examples.

questions.question: What does mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) measure?

options.text: The average pixel accuracy across images
The average per-class overlap between predicted and ground-truth masks
The mean training loss
The variance of predictions

questions.explanation: mIoU averages IoU over classes; it is the standard segmentation metric because it is robust to class imbalance.

questions.question: What key architectural change did Fully Convolutional Networks (FCN) introduce compared to earlier sliding-window CNN approaches to segmentation?

options.text: They replaced all convolutional layers with fully connected layers
They replaced the final fully connected layers with convolutional layers, enabling end-to-end dense prediction on arbitrary-sized inputs
They used only 1×1 convolutions throughout the entire network
They removed all pooling layers to preserve spatial resolution

questions.explanation: FCN's breakthrough was converting classification networks (e.g., VGG) into fully convolutional ones by replacing the dense layers with 1×1 convolutions and adding learnable upsampling (transposed convolutions). This allows the network to accept any input size and produce a dense, per-pixel prediction map in a single forward pass — unlike sliding-window methods that classified each patch independently.

questions.question: A segmentation model has an output stride (OS) of 16. What does this mean, and what is the primary trade-off when reducing it to OS=8?

options.text: The output is 16× larger than the input; reducing to OS=8 halves memory usage
The output feature map is 1/16 the spatial resolution of the input; reducing to OS=8 doubles spatial resolution but roughly quadruples computation and memory
The model takes 16 strides per convolution; OS=8 makes it faster by taking fewer strides
The model has 16 output classes; OS=8 means fewer classes are predicted

questions.explanation: Output stride is the ratio of input spatial resolution to the deepest feature map resolution. OS=16 means a 512×512 input produces a 32×32 feature map. Reducing to OS=8 (e.g., by replacing a stride-2 layer with an atrous convolution at rate 2) doubles the feature map to 64×64, which improves boundary localization — but the feature map has 4× more spatial elements, so both memory and compute roughly quadruple. DeepLab typically uses OS=16 for training and OS=8 for evaluation as a practical compromise.

questions.question: The Tversky loss generalizes the Dice loss with two parameters α and β that weight false positives and false negatives differently. In medical image segmentation where missing a lesion is far more dangerous than a false alarm, which parameter setting is most appropriate?

options.text: α = 0.5, β = 0.5 (equal weighting, identical to Dice)
α = 0.7, β = 0.3 (penalize false positives more heavily than false negatives)
α = 0.3, β = 0.7 (penalize false negatives more heavily than false positives)
α = 1.0, β = 0.0 (ignore false negatives entirely)

questions.explanation: The Tversky index is TI = TP / (TP + α·FP + β·FN). When β > α, the denominator grows faster for false negatives, so the loss penalizes missed detections more than false alarms. In medical imaging, a missed lesion (FN) can be life-threatening, so we set α < β (e.g., 0.3 / 0.7) to push the model toward higher recall at the expense of some precision. Setting α = β = 0.5 recovers the standard Dice coefficient, which treats FP and FN symmetrically.

questions.question: Dense CRF post-processing typically improves segmentation boundary quality by modeling pairwise pixel relationships. What is the primary reason this technique is often skipped in real-time segmentation pipelines?

options.text: CRF requires ground-truth labels at inference time
CRF inference adds 100–500 ms per image due to iterative mean-field approximation, which exceeds real-time latency budgets
CRF only works with binary (two-class) segmentation masks
CRF always degrades mIoU because it over-smooths small objects

questions.explanation: Dense CRF uses iterative mean-field inference with bilateral and Gaussian pairwise potentials, which refines boundaries by encouraging nearby pixels with similar color to share the same label. While this can boost mIoU by 2-5%, each iteration involves message passing across all pixel pairs (approximated via high-dimensional filtering), adding 100-500ms per image. For real-time applications targeting 30+ FPS (~33ms per frame), this overhead is prohibitive. Modern alternatives include boundary-aware losses (e.g., boundary Dice) or lightweight learned CRF modules like ConvCRF that trade global pairwise reasoning for speed.

questions.question: Transposed convolution (also called deconvolution) is commonly used in U-Net decoders for learnable upsampling. However, a well-known artifact can degrade output quality. What is it, and what is the recommended alternative?

options.text: Transposed convolution produces 'checkerboard artifacts' caused by uneven overlap of the kernel during upsampling; the recommended fix is bilinear upsampling followed by a regular convolution
Transposed convolution introduces 'border replication artifacts' at image edges; the fix is to apply zero-padding before each upsampling step
Transposed convolution always doubles the channel dimension unintentionally; the fix is to add a 1×1 convolution before each transposed conv to halve the channels first
Transposed convolution produces 'aliasing artifacts' identical to those in standard max-pooling; bilinear downsampling avoids the issue upstream

questions.explanation: Transposed convolution upsamples by inserting zeros between input pixels and convolving with a learned kernel. When the kernel size is not divisible by the stride (e.g., 3×3 kernel with stride 2), different output pixels receive contributions from different numbers of kernel weights — some pixels accumulate more gradient and become brighter, creating a characteristic checkerboard or grid pattern in the output. Odena et al. (2016, 'Deconvolution and Checkerboard Artifacts') showed this is inherent to the operation. The standard practitioner fix is to use bilinear upsampling (nearest-neighbor also works) to resize the feature map, then apply a regular 3×3 or 1×1 convolution to learn spatial transformations — this decouples the upsampling geometry from the learned weights and eliminates uneven overlap. TensorFlow: `tf.keras.layers.UpSampling2D(size=(2,2), interpolation='bilinear')` followed by `Conv2D`.

questions.question: BiSeNet achieves real-time segmentation by splitting the network into two pathways. What is the role of each pathway?

options.text: One pathway processes RGB channels and the other processes depth channels
A spatial path preserves high-resolution spatial detail while a context path captures rich semantic information at lower resolution
One pathway runs on CPU and the other runs on GPU for hardware parallelism
Both pathways are identical but process the image at different crop positions

questions.explanation: BiSeNet's bilateral design separates the competing demands of segmentation: the spatial path uses a small, shallow network that preserves 1/8 resolution for fine boundary detail, while the context path uses a deep backbone (e.g., ResNet-18) with rapid downsampling for large receptive fields and high-level semantics. A Feature Fusion Module merges both, achieving 68.4% mIoU on Cityscapes at 105 FPS — demonstrating that decoupling spatial and semantic processing is more efficient than a single compromise architecture.

questions.question: Panoptic segmentation unifies semantic and instance segmentation. What is the key distinction between 'stuff' and 'things' classes in the panoptic framework, and how does this affect the output format?

options.text: 'Stuff' classes (sky, road) are amorphous regions assigned per-pixel labels only, while 'things' classes (car, person) receive both a class label and a unique instance ID per connected object
'Stuff' refers to moving objects and 'things' refers to static background — the model outputs separate masks for each
'Stuff' and 'things' are interchangeable terms — every pixel gets an instance ID regardless of class
'Stuff' classes are predicted at half resolution and 'things' at full resolution to save compute

questions.explanation: In panoptic segmentation (Kirillov et al., 2019), 'stuff' classes are uncountable amorphous regions (sky, grass, road) where individual instances don't make semantic sense — they only need per-pixel class labels. 'Things' classes are countable objects (car, person, dog) that require both a class label and a unique instance ID to distinguish separate objects of the same class. The output is a panoptic map where each pixel has a (class_id, instance_id) tuple, with instance_id = 0 for stuff classes. The Panoptic Quality (PQ) metric evaluates both simultaneously: PQ = SQ × RQ (Segmentation Quality × Recognition Quality).

questions.question: DeepLab v3's Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) uses parallel atrous convolutions at rates {6, 12, 18} plus a 1×1 convolution and global average pooling. Why does ASPP include the global average pooling branch, and what problem does it address?

options.text: Global average pooling reduces memory usage by compressing the feature map to a single vector before the final classifier

At very high dilation rates, atrous convolutions degenerate — the kernel samples only a few effective pixels — so global average pooling provides a complementary image-level feature that captures full-image context
Global average pooling is needed to normalize the outputs of the different atrous branches to the same scale before concatenation
It replaces the CRF post-processing step by providing global smoothing within the network itself

questions.explanation: As the dilation rate increases, the effective number of kernel weights that fall on valid feature map locations decreases — at extreme rates, a 3×3 atrous convolution degenerates toward a 1×1 convolution (the 'gridding problem'). This means the highest-rate branches in ASPP may not effectively capture the global context they're designed for. The image-level global average pooling branch addresses this by collapsing the entire feature map into a single vector (then upsampled back), providing a guaranteed global context signal regardless of dilation artifacts. Chen et al. (2017) showed this branch contributes 0.5–1.0% mIoU improvement on PASCAL VOC 2012, confirming that explicit global features complement the multi-scale atrous branches.
